newsitem.title: INDIA: India's chemical sector seeks overseas tie-ups.
newsitem.headline: India's chemical sector seeks overseas tie-ups.

text.p: India's booming chemicals industry is seeking overseas partners to help it modernise to meet the challenge of economic reforms, industry officials said.

Kawas Bharucha, managing director of Colour-Chem, said labour, technical manpower, raw material and the capital cost of setting up a plant in India were comparatively lower than in other countries of the world.

"The fact that the global dyestuff industry is shifting from high-cost low-growth areas to low-cost high-growth areas, has opened up undreamt of opportunities for India," Bharucha, whose firm is a subsidiary of Germany's Hoechst A.G., said.
He was speaking at a two-day chemicals markets conference that ended on Tuesday.
N.R. Banerji, secretary of India's department of chemicals and petrochemicals, said the main thrust in the chemical sector was modernisation aimed at improving efficiency by lowering operating costs.
"With the liberalised policy of the government, it is expected that closely held technologies in certain areas would now be available," he said.
Foreign firms have shown keen interest in India's chemical sector, one of the fastest growing industries at over 10 percent annually under the impetus of economic reforms that began in 1991.

"The chemicals industry has grown faster than the industrial sector as a whole and is likely to have a 15-20 percent growth rate in the future," said Nicholas Butt, head of investment banking at Jardine Fleming India Securities Pvt. Ltd.
Foreign investors have flooded into India since 1991, and many more are queueing up.
India's chemical industry is the biggest beneficiary of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), Butt said, accounting for 20 percent of FDI inflows of about $1.3 billion by the end of 1994/95 (April-March).
Banerji said the average annual growth in India's petrochemicals sector during the last three years has ranged between 12 percent and 15 percent. It is expected to stay at those levels.

"Foreign chemical companies have the technological know-how and experience to make Indian industries more competitive and environmentally friendly," Bruce Moore, president of Eastman Chemical Asia Pacific Pte Ltd, said.
He warned overseas investors to ensure their India strategy fitted into their company's overall global strategy, advising them to be prepared to drive basic change in the marketplace.

"The coatings industry is an example of this," he said. "The value of putting quality paints on houses, cars, appliances and furniture is not widely understood in India. These markets have to be developed through educational and promotional programmes."
